::: {.callout-note .objectives title="Learning objectives"}
* Use `group_by()` with `summarise()` to compute summary values for groups of
  observations
* Use `count()` to count the numbers of observations within categories
* Combine data from two tables based on a common identifier (`join`
  operations)
* Customize plots created using ggplot2 by changing labels, scales and
  colours
:::

# Grouping and combining data

* More **dplyr**: summarising by group, and joining tables that hold data on the
  same observational unit from different sources
* Then back to **ggplot2** -- labels, scales, colours
* Both are core tidyverse, loaded by `library(tidyverse)`

```{r}
#| label: library_tidyverse
library(tidyverse)
```

```{r}
#| label: load_metabric
#| message: false
metabric <- read_csv("data/metabric_clinical_and_expression_data.csv")
metabric
```

# Grouping observations

## Summaries for groups

* Recap: `summarise()` over all rows

```{r}
#| label: summarise_mean_esr1
summarise(metabric, mean(ESR1))
```

* Real power is per-group -- the alternative is filtering each category by hand
* Two ways: `group_by()` or the **`.by`** argument

```{r}
#| label: group_by_er_status
metabric |>
    group_by(ER_status) |>
    summarise(mean(ESR1))
```

or

```{r}
#| label: summarise_by_argument
metabric |>
    summarise(mean(ESR1), .by = ER_status)
```

::: {.showimg}
![](assets/imgs/session6/group_and_summarise.png)

Show **the group and summarise diagram** here
:::

* Extra column for the grouping variable, one row per category
* With a single grouping column the two methods are identical
* Sanity check -- ER+ should be higher; values are log~2~, so the difference is a
  fold change

```{r}
#| label: fold_change_calculation
2 ^ (10.6 - 6.21)  # equivalent to (2 ^ 10.6) / (2 ^ 6.21)
```

* Group by two columns -- now `group_by()` and `.by` differ

```{r}
#| label: group_by_two_variables
metabric |>
    group_by(ER_status, Cancer_type) |>
    summarise(mean(ERBB2))
```

* `summarise()` peels off the **last** grouping only -- tibble is still grouped by
  `ER_status`, and that affects everything downstream
* `slice_max()` -- top n rows ranked by a named column

```{r}
#| label: slice_max_grouped
metabric |>
    group_by(ER_status, Cancer_type) |>
    summarise(ERBB2_mean = mean(ERBB2)) |>
    slice_max(ERBB2_mean, n = 1)
```

* Asked for one row, got two -- the retained grouping is why
* **`ungroup()`** to drop it

```{r}
#| label: ungroup_before_slice_max
metabric |>
    group_by(ER_status, Cancer_type) |>
    summarise(ERBB2_mean = mean(ERBB2)) |>
    ungroup() |>
    slice_max(ERBB2_mean, n = 1)
```

* With `.by` the grouping is dropped automatically after the summarise

```{r}
#| label: summarise_by_two_variables
metabric |>
    summarise(ERBB2_mean = mean(ERBB2), .by = c(ER_status, Cancer_type))
```

* Also: `group_by()` sorts by the grouping columns, `.by` does not
* `.by` is generally simpler -- no `ungroup()` to remember
* Per-operation grouping works in other verbs too
* Gotcha: `mutate()`, `filter()`, `summarise()` use **`.by`**; `slice_max()` and
  relatives use plain **`by`**

```{r}
#| label: slice_max_by_argument
metabric |>
    summarise(ERBB2_mean = mean(ERBB2), .by = c(ER_status, Cancer_type)) |>
    slice_max(ERBB2_mean, n = 1, by = ER_status)
```

* `summarise(across())` from last session -- several columns at once

```{r}
#| label: summarise_across_by_pam50
metabric |>
    summarise(across(c(ESR1, PGR, ERBB2), mean), .by = PAM50)
```

```{r}
#| label: summarise_across_two_groups
metabric |>
    summarise(across(c(ESR1, PGR, ERBB2), mean), .by = c(PAM50, HER2_status))
```

* **`n()`** -- counts rows rather than summarising a column

```{r}
#| label: summarise_group_sizes
metabric |>
    summarise(N = n(), ESR1_mean = mean(ESR1), .by = c(PAM50, HER2_status))
```

## Counts

* **`count()`** -- shorthand for the same thing

```{r}
#| label: count_pam50
count(metabric, PAM50)
```

* Like `table()`, but returns a tibble so it pipes onwards

```{r}
#| label: count_two_variables
count(metabric, PAM50, HER2_status)
```

* Count column is `n` by default; rename with `name =`

```{r}
#| label: count_with_name
count(metabric, PAM50, HER2_status, name = "Samples")
```

* The long-winded equivalent

```{r}
#| label: count_summarise_equivalent
#| eval: false
metabric |>
    summarize(Samples = n(), .by = c(PAM50, HER2_status))
```

* Always show `n` alongside a summary -- tells you if a mean rests on 3 samples

## Missing values

* Most summary functions return `NA` if any value is `NA` -- **`NA` propagation**

```{r}
#| label: summarise_missing_values
metabric |>
    summarize(N = n(),
              `Average tumour size` = mean(Tumour_size),
              .by = ER_status)
```

* `na.rm = TRUE` excludes them

```{r}
#| label: summarise_na_rm
metabric |>
    summarize(N = n(),
              `Average tumour size` = mean(Tumour_size, na.rm = TRUE),
              .by = ER_status)
```

* Filtering instead changes what `N` means -- may or may not be what you want

```{r}
#| label: filter_out_missing_values
metabric |>
    filter(!is.na(Tumour_size)) |>
    summarize(N = n(),
              `Average tumour size` = mean(Tumour_size),
              .by = ER_status)
```

## Counts and proportions

* `sum()` and `mean()` on **logical** vectors -- count of `TRUE`, proportion `TRUE`

```{r}
#| label: summarise_count_missing
metabric |>
    summarize(N = n(),
              Missing = sum(is.na(Tumour_size)),
              `Average tumour size` = mean(Tumour_size, na.rm = TRUE),
              .by = ER_status)
```

* Why it works: `is.na()` returns a logical vector

```{r}
#| label: is_na_test_vector
test_vector <- c(1, 3, 2, NA, 6, 5, NA, 10)
is.na(test_vector)
```

* **Coercion** -- `FALSE` is `0`, `TRUE` is `1`, so `sum()` counts

```{r}
#| label: sum_is_na
sum(is.na(test_vector))
```

```{r}
#| label: mean_is_na
mean(is.na(test_vector))
```

```{r}
#| label: summarise_proportion_missing
metabric |>
    summarize(N = n(),
              `Missing tumour size` = sum(is.na(Tumour_size)),
              `Proportion missing` = mean(is.na(Tumour_size)),
              .by = ER_status)
```

* Works for **any** condition returning a logical vector, not just `is.na()`

```{r}
#| label: summarise_proportion_long_survival
metabric |>
    filter(Survival_status == "DECEASED") |>
    summarise(N = n(),
              N_long_survival = sum(Survival_time > 120),
              Proportion_long_survival = mean(Survival_time > 120),
              .by = ER_status)
```

## Selecting or counting distinct things

* New data set: mutations from targeted sequencing of 173 genes
* Key point -- **multiple rows per observational unit** (many mutations per sample)

```{r}
#| label: load_mutations
#| message: false
mutations <- read_csv("data/metabric_mutations.csv")

select(mutations,
       Patient_ID,
       Chromosome,
       Position = Start_Position,
       Ref = Reference_Allele,
       Alt = Tumor_Seq_Allele1,
       Type = Variant_Type,
       Gene)
```

* Point out the first two rows -- same gene, same patient
* **`distinct()`** -- one row per value (or combination) of the given columns

```{r}
#| label: distinct_patients
mutations |>
    distinct(Patient_ID) |>
    nrow()
```

```{r}
#| label: count_mutations_per_patient
count(mutations, Patient_ID)
```

```{r}
#| label: count_mutations_per_gene
count(mutations, Gene)
```

* Patients per gene, not mutations per gene -- `distinct()` first, then `count()`

```{r}
#| label: count_patients_per_gene
mutations |>
    distinct(Patient_ID, Gene) |>
    count(Gene)
```

* Genes differing between the two tables are those mutated twice in one patient

```{r}
#| label: count_by_patient_and_chromosome
mutations |>
    count(Patient_ID, Chromosome)
```

# Joining data

* Data usually spread across tables from different sources
* dplyr joins combine two tables on matching values in a shared column -- same
  idea as SQL joins

## `left_join`

::: {.showimg}
![](assets/imgs/session6/dplyr_left_join.png)

Show **the left join diagram** here
:::

* `left_join()` keeps **all** rows of the left table; unmatched rows get `NA` in
  the new columns
* Toy example: Ugandan park animals and what they eat
* **RDS** -- R's own format for one saved object; read with `read_rds()`

```{r}
#| label: load_animal_tables
animals <- read_rds("data/animals.rds")
animal_diets <- read_rds("data/animal_diets.rds")
```

* **`by`** takes the matching column name as a string

```{r}
#| label: left_join_animals
animals
animal_diets
left_join(animals, animal_diets, by = "animal")
```

* Lion: in left only -> kept, `eats` is `NA`
* Hippo: in right only -> dropped
* `NA` means "not recorded here", not "lions don't eat"
* `right_join()` -- all rows of the right table; rarely used

```{r}
#| label: right_join_animals
right_join(animals, animal_diets, by = "animal")
```

## `inner_join`

* Only observations present in **both** tables

::: {.showimg}
![](assets/imgs/session6/dplyr_inner_join.png)

Show **the inner join diagram** here
:::

```{r}
#| label: inner_join_animals
inner_join(animals, animal_diets, by = "animal")
```

## `full_join`

* Everything from both tables, `NA` filling the gaps

::: {.showimg}
![](assets/imgs/session6/dplyr_full_join.png)

Show **the full join diagram** here
:::

```{r}
#| label: full_join_animals
full_join(animals, animal_diets, by = "animal")
```

* Both lion and hippo now present

## Joining on columns with different headers

* Matching columns named differently in each table -- use **`join_by()`**
* Column names inside `join_by()` are **unquoted**, tidyverse style

```{r}
#| label: join_different_column_names
animal_diets2 <- read_rds("data/animal_diets2.rds")
animal_diets2
left_join(animals, animal_diets2, by = join_by(animal == species))
```

* Left table's name wins in the output -- `animal`, not `species`

## Multiple matches in join operations

* What if the thing being joined appears more than once?

```{r}
#| label: join_multiple_matches_right
extra_food <- tibble(animal = "elephant", eats = "fruit")
animal_diets3 <- bind_rows(animal_diets, extra_food)
animal_diets3
left_join(animals, animal_diets3, by = "animal")
```

* Duplicated on **both** sides -> all combinations

```{r}
#| label: join_multiple_matches_both
extra_park <- tibble(animal = "elephant", park = "Kibale")
animals3 <- bind_rows(animals, extra_park)
animals3
left_join(animals3, animal_diets3, by = "animal")
```

* Point out the **many-to-many** warning -- 2 x 2 = 4 rows
* Usually a symptom of unexpected duplicates in the data
* Silence it only if it really is intended

```{r}
#| label: join_many_to_many
left_join(animals3,
          animal_diets3,
          by = "animal",
          relationship = "many-to-many")
```

## Joining by matching on multiple columns

* List several columns in `join_by()` when the unit needs more than one to
  identify it

```{r}
#| label: join_on_multiple_columns
animal_species <- read_rds("data/animal_species.rds")
species_diets <- read_rds("data/species_diets.rds")

animal_species
species_diets

full_join(animal_species, species_diets, by = join_by(genus, species))
```

* Lion and leopard share genus `Panthera` -- joining on genus alone mismatches them

## Clashing column names

* Non-join columns with the same name in both tables get a **suffix**

```{r}
#| label: join_clashing_column_names
animal_survey <- read_rds("data/animal_survey.rds")
diet_survey <- read_rds("data/diet_survey.rds")

animal_survey
diet_survey

left_join(animal_survey, diet_survey, by = "animal")
```

* Better to rename or drop them before joining

## A real example: joining the METABRIC clinical and mRNA expression data

* This is how the combined file used all week was actually built

```{r}
#| label: load_clinical_data
#| message: false
clinical_data <- read_csv("data/metabric_clinical_data.csv")
clinical_data <- select(clinical_data, Patient_ID, ER_status, PAM50)
clinical_data
```

```{r}
#| label: load_mrna
#| message: false
mrna_expression_data <- read_tsv("data/metabric_mrna_expression.txt")
mrna_expression_data
```

* `inner_join()` -- only patients with expression data; ID columns named
  differently, so `join_by()`

```{r}
#| label: join_clinical_and_mrna
combined_data <- inner_join(clinical_data,
                            mrna_expression_data,
                            by = join_by(Patient_ID == SAMPLE_ID))
combined_data
```

```{r}
#| label: box_plot_1
combined_data |>
    filter(!is.na(PAM50), !is.na(ESR1)) |>
    ggplot(mapping = aes(x = PAM50, y = ESR1, colour = PAM50)) +
    geom_boxplot(show.legend = FALSE)
```

# Customizing plots with ggplot2

## Titles and labels

* `labs()` -- name-value pairs; any aesthetic plus `title`, `subtitle`, `caption`

```{r}
#| label: scatter_plot_1
ggplot(metabric, mapping = aes(x = GATA3, y = ESR1, colour = ER_status)) +
    geom_point(size = 0.6, alpha = 0.5) +
    geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
    labs(title = "mRNA expression in the METABRIC breast cancer data set",
         subtitle = "Expression measured with Illumina bead arrays",
         x = "log2 GATA3 expression",
         y = "log2 ESR1 expression",
         colour = "ER status")
```

* Labels are another element of the plot object, alongside mappings and layers
* Naming the `colour` aesthetic is what tidies the legend title

## Scales

* ggplot2 picks scales from the data type: continuous for `GATA3`/`ESR1`,
  discrete for `ER_status`
* Add **scale layers** to override; naming convention:

```
scale_<NAME_OF_AESTHETIC>_<NAME_OF_SCALE>
```

* Show the `scale_y_continuous` help page
* `breaks` -- where ticks and labels go

```{r}
#| label: scatter_plot_2
ggplot(data = metabric,
       mapping = aes(x = GATA3, y = ESR1, colour = ER_status)) +
    geom_point(size = 0.6, alpha = 0.5) +
    geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
    scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(5, 15, by = 2.5))
```

* `seq()` -- regular sequences, from/to/by

```{r}
#| label: seq_breaks
seq(5, 15, by = 2.5)
```

* `limits` -- axis extents; deliberately clipped here, expect the "removed rows"
  warning

```{r}
#| label: scatter_plot_3
ggplot(data = metabric,
       mapping = aes(x = GATA3, y = ESR1, colour = ER_status)) +
    geom_point(size = 0.6, alpha = 0.5) +
    geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
    scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(5, 15, by = 2.5), limits = c(4, 12))
```

* **`theme()`** controls the non-data components

```{r}
#| label: scatter_plot_4
ggplot(data = metabric,
       mapping = aes(x = GATA3, y = ESR1, colour = ER_status)) +
    geom_point(size = 0.6, alpha = 0.5) +
    theme(panel.grid = element_blank())
```

* Not covered further; prebuilt themes exist, plus packages like *ggtheme*

```{r}
#| label: scatter_plot_5
ggplot(data = metabric,
       mapping = aes(x = GATA3, y = ESR1, colour = ER_status)) +
    geom_point(size = 0.6, alpha = 0.5) +
    theme_minimal()
```

## Colours

* Default for a categorical variable is `scale_colour_discrete`; override with
  `scale_colour_manual`

```{r}
#| label: scatter_plot_6
ggplot(data = metabric,
       mapping = aes(x = GATA3, y = ESR1, colour = ER_status)) +
    geom_point(size = 0.6, alpha = 0.5) +
    geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c("dodgerblue2", "firebrick2"))
```

* **Name the values** to control which colour goes with which category

```{r}
#| label: scatter_plot_7
ggplot(data = metabric,
       mapping = aes(x = GATA3, y = ESR1, colour = ER_status)) +
    geom_point(size = 0.6, alpha = 0.5) +
    geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c(Positive = "dodgerblue2",
                                   Negative = "firebrick2"))
```

* Manual is fine for two or three categories; beyond that use a palette
* ColorBrewer palettes via `scale_colour_brewer()` / `scale_fill_brewer()`

```{r}
#| label: scatter_plot_8
ggplot(data = metabric,
       mapping = aes(x = GATA3, y = ESR1, colour = `3-gene_classifier`)) +
    geom_point(size = 0.6, alpha = 0.5, na.rm = TRUE) +
    scale_colour_brewer(palette = "Set1")
```

* Point at `?scale_colour_brewer` and colorbrewer2.org
* Gotcha: unnamed `labels` are matched in **data order**, not the order you typed
  -- mislabelled legend

```{r}
#| label: scatter_plot_9
ggplot(data = metabric,
       mapping = aes(x = GATA3, y = ESR1, colour = ER_status)) +
    geom_point(size = 0.6, alpha = 0.5) +
    geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c(Positive = "dodgerblue2",
                                   Negative = "firebrick2"),
                        labels = c(Positive = "ER-positive",
                                   Negative = "ER-negative"))
```

* Continuous variable -> colour **gradient**, not discrete palette

```{r}
#| label: scatter_plot_10
ggplot(data = metabric,
       mapping = aes(x = GATA3,
                     y = ESR1,
                     colour = Nottingham_prognostic_index)) +
    geom_point(size = 0.6, alpha = 0.5)
```

* Default is black-to-blue; high NPI = worse prognosis, so emphasise it in red

```{r}
#| label: scatter_plot_11
metabric |>
    ggplot(mapping = aes(x = GATA3,
                         y = ESR1,
                         colour = Nottingham_prognostic_index)) +
    geom_point(size = 0.75) +
    scale_colour_gradient(low = "white", high = "red")
```

* `scale_colour_gradient2()` -- diverging, two gradients about a `midpoint`

```{r}
#| label: scatter_plot_12
metabric |>
    ggplot(mapping = aes(x = GATA3,
                         y = ESR1,
                         colour = Nottingham_prognostic_index)) +
    geom_point(size = 0.75) +
    scale_colour_gradient2(low = "dodgerblue1",
                           mid = "grey90",
                           high = "firebrick1",
                           midpoint = 4.5)
```

# Summary

* Computing summary values for groups of observations
* Counting the numbers of observations within categories
* Combining data from two tables through join operations
* Customizing plots created with ggplot2 by changing labels, scales and colours
